title: Ellyse Perry's Rapid Fifty Lifts Australia to Nervy Two-Wicket Win Over New Zealand
excerpt: Australia chased 163 to win the first T20I at North Sydney Oval by two wickets with seven balls to spare, despite slipping to 145 for 7 after Ellyse Perry's 52 off 30 balls.
body:
• Ellyse Perry hit 52 off 30 balls as Australia chased 163 to beat New Zealand by two wickets with seven balls to spare in the first T20I at North Sydney Oval.
  • New Zealand posted 162 for 2, built on Georgia Plimmer's career-best 85 not out off 68 balls and Maddy Green's unbeaten 56 off 37.
  • Australia slumped to 145 for 7 in the 16th over before captain Sophie Molineux and Kim Garth finished the chase, Garth hitting the winning boundary.
  • Australia lead the three-match series 1-0, with two matches remaining for a new-look New Zealand side missing retired stars Sophie Devine, Suzie Bates and Lea Tahuhu.

Perry sets up a chase Australia nearly threw away

Australia beat New Zealand by two wickets in the first women's T20I at North Sydney Oval on Sunday, chasing down 163 with seven balls to spare in their first T20 match since winning the World Cup in July. Ellyse Perry made 52 off 30 balls, reaching her half-century off 27 deliveries, according to ESPNcricinfo's match report. The win gives Australia a 1-0 lead in the three-match series.

The chase began badly. Georgia Voll was trapped lbw by left-arm seamer Bree Illing on the second ball, reviewing only to fall on umpire's call. Perry and Beth Mooney then rebuilt at speed, adding 86 for the second wicket with regular boundaries on a flat surface. Mooney made 38 off 25 balls despite removing her contact lenses early in her innings, before she was run out in unusual fashion, setting off for a run that was not there amid a loud lbw appeal.

Perry kept going, bringing up fifty with a straight drive, but she then hit a Jess Kerr long hop straight to deep backward square. From there the innings unravelled. Ashleigh Gardner fell lbw to Kerr on review, Nicola Carey was run out in a mix-up, and Australia slipped to 145 for 7 in the 16th over. Kerr finished with 3 for 25 from four overs.

Plimmer and Green carry New Zealand

Sent in to bat, New Zealand lost Flora Devonshire early, bowled through the gate by a Kim Garth inswinger, and captain Amelia Kerr for 9, caught off Annabel Sutherland. At 35 for 2, the innings rested on Georgia Plimmer and Maddy Green.

Plimmer, who had been dropped during New Zealand's disappointing World Cup campaign, made a career-best 85 not out off 68 balls. She reached fifty off 40 balls and shifted gears after a slow start. Green, the side's most experienced player on the day, struck an unbeaten 56 off 37 balls, including 14 runs in three balls off Carey late in the innings. Their unbroken stand took New Zealand to 162 for 2 from 20 overs. Sutherland took 1 for 28 and Garth 1 for 34 for Australia.

Plimmer was named player of the match despite finishing on the losing side. She had also been given lives on 15 and 39, when Mooney missed a stumping and dropped a catch while keeping up to the stumps, the IANS report noted.

A finish that exposed Australia's rust

Australia's fielding and lower-order batting looked short of match practice. Lucy Hamilton, recalled after a hip injury ahead of Megan Schutt, finished with 0 for 23 from two overs, although she took a diving catch at fine leg to dismiss Amelia Kerr.

At the end, captain Sophie Molineux took Australia to the brink before she was bowled by Rosemary Mair attempting a lap sweep, with four runs still needed and only two wickets left. Kim Garth settled it, square-driving her first scoring shot to the boundary to complete a 165 for 8 finish in 18.5 overs.

New Zealand's defeat came with positives. Illing was dangerous with the new ball, Jess Kerr struck at key moments, and Plimmer and Green showed the batting can function without Devine, Bates and Tahuhu. The cost: Amelia Kerr conceded 50 in four overs, the most expensive figures of her T20I career.

What it means for the series

Australia were without Phoebe Litchfield, ruled out with a hip injury, and replaced her with Tahlia McGrath in their only change from the side that beat England in the World Cup final. The result keeps their winning run in the format intact, but the manner of it — eight wickets lost chasing a target their top order had under control — gives New Zealand a workable plan for the remaining two matches: survive Perry and Mooney, then attack a middle order that showed it can panic.

For New Zealand, the task is conversion. Finishing on 162 for 2 with two set batters unbeaten suggests runs were left in the innings by accelerating late rather than early.
